_comment: Plain-language rendering of the engine verdict, at two densities: `short` is the one line the page leads with, `detail` is the paraphrase behind 'more info'. `quote` is verbatim from the named deliverable and is NEVER translated — a citation in translation is not a citation. Canonical EN, mirrored in frontend/src/i18n/locales/*.ts (short+detail, translated) and frontend/src/i18n/narrativeSources.ts (quote+source, EN); a vitest fails on drift. The verdict leads with the ILCD situation (D4.1 Table 1), the variable the deliverables use; the IS-01..IS-05 pathways, a T4.6 construct the deliverables do not know, were removed on 2026-10-18. Every quote is checked verbatim against the source document, and its section number against the section that actually contains it, by scripts/verify_citations.py.

ILCD Situation A.title: Decision support with limited consequences (ILCD Situation A)
ILCD Situation A.short: Micro-level decision support: the exchange is too small to change the background system. Attributional modelling, with substitution against the average market mix.
ILCD Situation A.detail: The exchange affects the actors involved, not what the wider economy produces or how. You therefore model with average, accounting-style data, and represent what the symbiosis displaces by substituting the average market mix — the national grid mix for electricity, average virgin production for a material. D4.1 warns explicitly against reaching for consequential modelling merely because a decision is being taken.
ILCD Situation A.quote: The decision (e.g., a synergy between two factories) has limited consequences. It does not cause large-scale, structural changes to the background system (e.g., it is too small to trigger the construction of new power plants or shift global market prices). Modeling Rule: Apply Attributional Modeling with Substitution.

ILCD Situation B.title: Decision support with structural consequences (ILCD Situation B)
ILCD Situation B.short: Meso/macro-level decision support: the decision causes structural change in the background system, so consequential modelling against the marginal technology. D4.1 asks you to prove that scale before choosing it.
ILCD Situation B.detail: The decision is large enough to shift installed capacity or the output of a specific technology. Modelling goes consequential, and what the symbiosis displaces is the marginal technology, identified through a market analysis rather than taken as the average mix. The burden of proof is on you: this route has to be demonstrated, not assumed.
ILCD Situation B.quote: Only apply full consequential modeling if you can prove the IS network will cause structural changes in the global or national economy (e.g., creates a demand so large it triggers new capacity installation outside the network).

ILCD Situation C1.title: Documenting an existing network (ILCD Situation C1)
ILCD Situation C1.short: Accounting with interactions — documenting what an existing network gives the wider economy. Substitution at the average market mix, as in Situation A.
ILCD Situation C1.detail: You are documenting a network that exists rather than supporting a decision, so the study is descriptive. But since the point is to show what the network gives the wider economy, multifunctionality is still resolved by substitution at the average market mix — operationally the same rule as Situation A.
ILCD Situation C1.quote: Situation C1 (Monitoring with Interactions): If the goal is to document the benefits of an existing IS network to the wider economy, use Substitution with the Average Market Mix (identical to Situation A).

ILCD Situation C2.title: Strict reporting of one company (ILCD Situation C2)
ILCD Situation C2.short: Strict accounting for one partner in isolation: allocation, and no substitution credits.
ILCD Situation C2.detail: Strict accounting for a single partner on its own, typically corporate reporting. Multifunctionality is resolved by allocation, and no credit is claimed for what the symbiosis displaces elsewhere: the number describes that partner's share of the burdens, not the benefit the network produces.
ILCD Situation C2.quote: Situation C2 (Strict Accounting): If the goal is strict corporate reporting for a specific partner in isolation, use Allocation (Step 3). Do not apply substitution credits.

deactivated.short: No economic analysis — the economic dimension is off in Q3.
deactivated.detail: Q3 has no economic dimension selected, so the engine configures no costing at all. If the case needs a business case — and for a symbiosis that has to be signed by several firms it usually does — go back to Q3 and switch the economic dimension on.

C+E.short: Conventional LCC (the firm's real cash flows) plus environmental LCC (the value chain, on the same boundary as the LCA).
C+E.detail: Two views run together. The conventional LCC answers whether it pays for the individual firm: real cash flows, taxes and fees as costs, subsidies as reductions. The environmental LCC widens the boundary to every actor in the life cycle and is kept consistent with the parallel LCA, so the two can be read side by side. Watch for double counting: a carbon or landfill tax already in the cash flows must not reappear as a monetised externality.
C+E.quote: Conventional LCC (C-LCC) — The Firm Perspective: Evaluates strict financial feasibility from the perspective of an individual actor, equivalent to a Total Cost of Ownership analysis. […] Environmental LCC (E-LCC) — The Value Chain Perspective: Provides an economic assessment directly consistent with a parallel LCA, expanding the boundary to cover all actors within the defined life cycle system.

C+E+S.short: Conventional and environmental LCC plus societal LCC: taxes and subsidies adjusted through the Net Tax Factor, environmental impacts monetised.
C+E+S.detail: On top of the firm and value-chain views comes the welfare view. Taxes and subsidies are transfers inside society rather than real costs to it, so they are excluded or converted into shadow prices through the Net Tax Factor, and the environmental impacts from the parallel LCA are monetised. This is the configuration a public decision needs, which is why a public or policy objective brings it in.
C+E+S.quote: Societal LCC (S-LCC) — The Welfare Perspective: Quantifies broader societal welfare implications. Taxes and subsidies are excluded or adjusted using a Net Tax Factor (NTF) to convert budget costs into shadow prices, since they represent transfers within society rather than net costs to it.

C-LCC.short: Conventional LCC only — the firm perspective, equivalent to a total cost of ownership analysis.
C-LCC.detail: Only the firm's own perspective. Every policy instrument is a real cash flow: taxes and fees are costs, subsidies reduce capex or opex. It is the right frame for corporate reporting, and it deliberately says nothing about value-chain or societal effects — claiming those would overstate what a single-actor account can support.
C-LCC.quote: Conventional LCC (C-LCC) — The Firm Perspective: Evaluates strict financial feasibility from the perspective of an individual actor, equivalent to a Total Cost of Ownership analysis. All policy instruments are modeled as real cash flows: taxes and fees are costs; subsidies are CAPEX or OPEX reductions.

C+N.short: Conventional LCC for each partner, consolidated at network level. No environmental LCC: the case has no LCA to keep it consistent with.
C+N.detail: Each firm's real cash flows first, then the same accounts added up across the network, where the payments between partners cancel out. The environmental LCC is left out because D4.2 builds it on the boundary of a parallel LCA, and the case assesses no environmental dimension. Switch the environmental dimension on in Q3 if the study needs the value-chain view.
C+N.quote: The C-LCC analysis must be conducted at two nested levels. The primary boundary is Gate-to-Gate, drawn around each individual participating firm. […] After individual firm analyses are complete, a secondary aggregated analysis is performed by expanding the boundary to Entry-to-Gate, encompassing the entire group of collaborating firms
C+N.source: D4.2 §4.1 — Boundary Definition by LCC Type

C+N+S.short: Conventional LCC per partner and for the network, plus societal LCC with the Net Tax Factor. Without an LCA, environmental impacts are not monetised.
C+N+S.detail: The firm and network accounts as above, plus the welfare view a public decision needs: taxes and subsidies converted through the Net Tax Factor, a social discount rate, and a boundary that reaches end of life. What is missing is the monetisation of environmental impacts, which needs the results of a parallel LCA: switch the environmental dimension on in Q3 to add it.
C+N+S.quote: When the study serves a public policy or territorial planning objective, the boundary must expand to Cradle-to-Grave to capture all costs to society, including end-of-life phases typically borne by municipalities or the public rather than by the firms themselves.
C+N+S.source: D4.2 §4.1 — Boundary Definition by LCC Type

active.short: S-LCA active: social indicators per stakeholder group.
active.detail: The social dimension is on. Each stakeholder group — workers, consumers, local communities, value-chain actors — is mapped to the processes it is affected by, and from there to impact subcategories and indicators. The mapping is only as good as the engagement behind it, so talking to the groups involved is part of the data collection, not an optional extra.
active.quote: The classification of stakeholders follows the UNEP/SETAC framework and is adapted to the characteristics of Industrial Symbiosis systems. The main stakeholder categories typically include workers, consumers, local communities and value chain actors, each associated with specific social aspects.

deactivated.short: S-LCA not activated — the social dimension is off in Q3.
deactivated.detail: Q3 has no social dimension selected, so no stakeholder mapping and no social indicator are configured. Switch it on in Q3 if the case has to say anything about workers or local communities — which is usually the case when a symbiosis is presented to a municipality or a community.
